analysis.one_liner: Sets steel and aluminum plants' groundwater cleanup standards at the property line instead of at each waste site.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the existing hazardous waste law, a steel or aluminum plant has to clean up groundwater to standards at each of its individual waste units. This bill would change that for steel and aluminum facilities only: the standards would have to be met at the plant's outer property line instead, with monitoring at the boundary and corrective action taken before contamination reached it. It would also require plant owners to set aside money to pay for monitoring and cleanup for 30 years after a plant shuts down.
analysis.who_benefits: Steel and aluminum plant owners would benefit most: they could leave groundwater between their waste units and the property line uncleaned to standards, as long as pollution does not reach the boundary, which cuts remediation costs. Neighbors and future users of the land also gain one protection the bill adds — a dedicated fund covering 30 years of monitoring and cleanup after a plant closes.

how_it_helps.text: Corrective measures would only have to assure that groundwater protection standards are met at the facility property boundary, rather than at each individual solid waste management unit, for steel (SIC 331) and aluminum (SIC 3334) plants. [S2][S3]
The bill requires groundwater monitoring at the facility property boundary and inside the facility, with corrective measures taken in advance of hazardous constituents reaching the boundary. [S3]

When a plant stops operating without removing all hazardous waste above the standards, the owner must establish a fund or other financial assurance adequate to cover monitoring and corrective measures for 30 years after closure. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: People living near steel and aluminum plants, and whoever uses the land or groundwater after a plant closes, bear the added risk: contamination under the plant property would not have to be cleaned to standards unless it approaches the boundary. The plant owners would pay to build and maintain the 30-year cleanup fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Neighbors of steel and aluminum plants

drawbacks.text: Measuring compliance only at the property boundary allows groundwater above protection standards to remain between waste units and the property line, and cleanup is triggered as contamination nears the boundary rather than at the source. [S2][S3]
The relaxed standard would apply only to facilities in two industry codes — steel (SIC 331) and aluminum (SIC 3334) — leaving other hazardous waste sites under stricter, unit-by-unit rules. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade: the 30-year financial responsibility requirement and expanded boundary monitoring impose real new costs on plant owners, which is why this was a negotiated package rather than pure relief. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a narrower cleanup obligation for plant owners against two real public protections — boundary monitoring with action before contamination escapes, and a 30-year cleanup fund after closure. But the central change, moving the compliance line from each waste unit to the property boundary, leaves contaminated groundwater in place under plant property, and the special treatment for just two industries is hard to justify on the merits. On balance it leans toward the plants, with meaningful but partial safeguards for the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Dave Durenberger introduced the bill on May 16, 1989, joined by Sens. Richard Lugar and Dan Coats, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. [S3][S5]
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991. [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel and aluminum plant owners avoided a new 30-year financial responsibility obligation, while neighbors kept the stricter existing rule that cleanup standards apply at each waste unit rather than only at the property line.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plant owners avoided new duties; neighbors kept old rules

for.name: Sen. Dave Durenberger
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to set steel and aluminum plants' groundwater cleanup standards at the facility property boundary with a 30-year post-closure fund.

for.name: Sens. Richard Lugar and Dan Coats
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick, D-ND)
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after referral; the action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred. The sponsor and original cosponsors were three Republicans, and two other Republicans plus one Democrat later signed on as cosponsors, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have relaxed where steel plants must meet groundwater cleanup standards — at the property line instead of at each waste unit — cutting remediation costs, while requiring them to fund 30 years of post-closure monitoring and corrective action. Their gain in cleanup flexibility came at the cost of leaving contamination in place under plant property.
The same trade-off would have applied to aluminum plants: a property-boundary compliance point that reduces cleanup obligations, paired with mandatory 30-year financial assurance after closure.
